identification.summary: DriftingCloud is the name Volexity uses for a Chinese APT actor it observed exploiting a then-unpatched Sophos Firewall authentication-bypass/remote-code-execution flaw (CVE-2022-1040) from early March 2022, about three weeks before the fix [S1][S2][S3]. The imported MISP Galaxy description characterizes it as a persistent actor that targets many industries and locations, develops or acquires zero-days, and commonly compromises gateway devices [S7].
identification.firstObserved: 2022-03 (Volexity-reported first exploitation of CVE-2022-1040, reported as 5 March 2022 by The Hacker News coverage) [S3].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name is mapped to DriftingCloud in the sources gathered. Trend Micro's 2023 ShadowPad research on Pakistani targets references 'DriftingCloud malware' in conference slides, but the sources reviewed do not state that Trend Micro attributes that intrusion to the Volexity DriftingCloud cluster; keep the two vendor contexts separate [S5][S6]. Volexity's primary blog post was not opened (host unreachable from this environment); details come from press coverage of it.

attribution.confidence: Volexity is reported to describe DriftingCloud as a Chinese APT group [S1][S3]. The sources gathered do not state a Volexity confidence level or tie the actor to a specific PRC agency or contractor.
attribution.basis: Press coverage of Volexity's June 2022 report; use of the Behinder web-shell framework, which coverage notes other Chinese groups also used against Confluence CVE-2022-26134, is cited as context, not as attribution proof [S2]. MISP Galaxy lists country CN [S7].

objectives: Volexity-reported activity indicates the firewall was an initial foothold; the actor aimed to breach cloud-hosted web servers hosting the victim's public websites and to intercept administrator CMS credentials and session cookies through DNS manipulation [S1][S2]. Broader strategic objectives are not stated in the sources gathered.

regions: South Asia (Sophos stated CVE-2022-1040 exploitation targeted a small set of specific organizations primarily in South Asia; this is a Sophos observation, not an attribution to DriftingCloud) [S4]
targeting.notes: Volexity's report described a single unnamed victim organization whose web properties were targeted [S1][S2]. Sector for that victim is not given in the coverage reviewed. The MISP Galaxy text says 'various industries and locations' without detail [S7].

capabilities.summary: Exploitation of Sophos Firewall CVE-2022-1040 (CVSS 9.8, affecting v18.5 MR3 and earlier) as a zero-day before the fix, with hotfixes starting 23 March 2022 [S1][S4]. Reported post-exploitation: web shells on the firewall reached via requests to a legitimate login.jsp file using the Behinder framework; creation of VPN user accounts with certificate pairs; DNS response modification for victim domains to enable man-in-the-middle capture of CMS admin credentials and session cookies; and deployment of PupyRAT, Pantegana and Sliver on web servers [S1][S2][S3].

campaigns.name: Sophos Firewall CVE-2022-1040 zero-day exploitation
campaigns.summary: Volexity reports DriftingCloud exploited the flaw from early March 2022, roughly three weeks before Sophos shipped hotfixes; Sophos's revised advisory said exploitation hit a small set of organizations primarily in South Asia [S1][S3][S4].

campaigns.name: Volexity publication: firewall breach leading to web-server and CMS compromise
campaigns.summary: Volexity detailed web shells, rogue VPN accounts, DNS response tampering for credential and cookie theft, and RAT deployment (PupyRAT, Pantegana, Sliver) on web servers behind the victim's firewall [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Trend Micro: possible supply-chain attack on Pakistani government delivering ShadowPad (context only)
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reported a trojanized installer of a Pakistani government application (E-Office) delivering ShadowPad to a government entity, a public sector bank and a telecom provider, and said it could not point to a particular group with confidence. Trend Micro slides mention 'DriftingCloud malware' on one victim; the link to Volexity's DriftingCloud is not established in the sources reviewed [S5][S6].

diamond.adversary: Chinese APT cluster named DriftingCloud by Volexity; sponsor and operators not identified in gathered sources [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: CVE-2022-1040 zero-day, Behinder web shell, rogue VPN accounts, DNS response tampering, PupyRAT, Pantegana, Sliver [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised Sophos Firewall appliances used as entry and pivot point; actor C2 details not captured in the coverage reviewed [S1][S2].
diamond.victim: One unnamed organization with cloud-hosted public web servers in Volexity's case; Sophos reports a small set of organizations primarily in South Asia [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Internet-exposed security gateway (firewall User Portal/Webadmin), CMS administration interfaces and DNS resolution trust [S1][S2][S4].

gaps: Volexity's primary report (volexity.com, 2022-06-15) could not be opened; all technical details come from secondary coverage and should be verified against it.
No Volexity confidence statement, PRC agency or contractor attribution, or Microsoft/MITRE mapping found.

Whether Trend Micro's 'DriftingCloud malware' reference in 2023 ShadowPad research concerns the same cluster as Volexity's DriftingCloud is unverified; Trend Micro said it could not attribute that intrusion to a particular group with confidence [S5][S6].

No alias list cited by a vendor source; MISP Galaxy and Malpedia synonym entries were not retrieved. A search-engine summary suggesting Tonto Team as an alias was not confirmed by any source and is not adopted.
Sector of the victim and all activity after mid-2022 are not documented in the sources gathered.
Sophos's South Asia targeting statement covers all CVE-2022-1040 exploitation, not necessarily only DriftingCloud.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing security gateways (firewall management portals) and the DNS and web/CMS tiers behind them are key cyber terrain. STEP 2: The actor exploited the gateway before a patch existed, so patch status alone is not protective; exposed management interfaces are the decisive variable [S1][S4]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is gateway zero-day, then web shell and rogue VPN accounts, then DNS tampering to harvest CMS credentials, then RAT deployment on web servers [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is repeated edge-device exploitation against South Asian and regional organizations. MDCOA is use of a gateway foothold to hijack DNS and credentials for onward access to partner or coalition web infrastructure. Candidate indicators: unexpected requests to login.jsp on the firewall, new VPN accounts and certificates, unexplained DNS answer changes, and Sliver or PupyRAT artifacts on web servers [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor advisories for edge devices and require management-interface exposure inventories. (2) Authorities: confirm who may direct emergency disabling of WAN-exposed administration portals on mission networks and partner-hosted services. (3) Mission assurance: plan fallback for DNS and web services if resolvers or gateways are suspect, and audit VPN account lists. (4) Coordination: share indicators with vendors and partner nations in South Asia; Sophos contacted affected organizations directly [S4].
